British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  This study examines how social support and affective factors (enjoyment, boredom, embarrassment, and shyness) shape young learners' informal digital learning of Chinese (IDLC) in New Zealand. Drawing on proactive language learning theory, we conceptualized IDLC as learners' autonomous involvement with Mandarin Chinese through digital technologies beyond the classroom. Survey data from 529 primary and secondary school students in Auckland were analysed using structural equation modelling. Results showed that social support significantly predicted IDLC both directly and indirectly via enjoyment as a partial mediator. Social support was also associated with higher enjoyment and lower levels of boredom and shyness, although these effects were modest. In contrast, boredom, embarrassment and shyness did not directly predict IDLC. These findings highlight the importance of supportive social environments and positive affect in fostering young learners' participation in out‐of‐class Chinese learning, while negative emotions appear less constraining in this context. The study extends informal language learning research to languages other than English and offers implications for Chinese language education in New Zealand.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            
                              Informal digital language learning has become an important complement to classroom‐based language instruction, particularly for young learners who regularly engage with digital media.
                            
                            
                              Social support from family members, peers and teachers is known to facilitate students' motivation and persistence in language learning.
                            
                            
                              Affective factors such as enjoyment, boredom, embarrassment and shyness influence learners' participation in second language learning, especially in formal classroom contexts.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            
                              This study extends research on informal digital language learning to Chinese as a target language other than English, focusing on young students in the New Zealand context.
                            
                            
                              It shows that social support and enjoyment are key predictors of IDLC, with enjoyment partially mediating the effect of social support.
                            
                            
                              The findings suggest that negative affective factors (boredom, embarrassment and shyness) do not directly constrain IDLC, highlighting important differences between formal classroom learning and informal digital learning environments.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and policy
                        
                          
                            
                              Teachers and schools can play an active role in legitimizing and encouraging IDLC by recognizing and valuing students' out‐of‐class digital engagement with Chinese.
                            
                            
                              Pedagogical efforts should prioritize fostering enjoyment by connecting classroom instruction with students' digital interests, such as short videos, music, games and online interaction.
                            
                            
                              Collaboration with families and community language schools can strengthen supportive learning ecologies that encourage informal digital learning.
                            
                            
                              Educational policies should view informal digital learning not as peripheral, but as a valuable extension of formal language education, particularly for languages with limited instructional time such as Chinese.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Multidimensional engagement effects of generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    adoption among minority ethnic international students in
                    <scp>UK</scp>
                    higher education
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has become a prevalent tool in higher education, yet little is known about how its use affects the learning experiences of minority‐ethnic international students (MEIS). Drawing on an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and a four‐strand engagement model, this quantitative study surveyed 273 MEIS across UK business schools and analysed the data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‐SEM). The findings suggest that performance expectancy, effort expectancy and social influence predicted intention, and facilitating conditions and intention were also positively associated with self‐reported GAI use frequency. GAI frequency positively predicted cognitive, behavioural, emotional and, most strongly, agentic engagement. Multigroup analysis revealed that female students showed stronger effects of effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions on intention than males; low‐experience students were more sensitive to effort expectancy than high‐experience peers; and postgraduate students exhibited stronger facilitating conditions, performance expectancy and social influence effects than undergraduates. The study highlights both theoretical and practical implications by linking GAI adoption with multidimensional student engagement, with the strongest association observed for agentic engagement, and calls for equity‐focused policy, curriculum interventions and institutional support targeted at individual access gaps among MEIS.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic?
                          
                            
                              Generative AI (GAI) technologies are increasingly used by students in higher education for learning support.
                            
                            
                              The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) has been widely applied to examine technology adoption in educational contexts.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds?
                          
                            
                              It extends UTAUT to an under‐researched population (MEIS), who often face heightened academic, technological and cultural challenges in UK higher education.
                            
                            
                              GAI use by MEIS is strongly associated with cognitive, behavioural, emotional and especially agentic engagement.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              Institutions should consider embedding GAI literacy and access support into orientation and academic skills programmes for MEIS.
                            
                            
                              Educators who integrate GAI into teaching may consider structured questioning, verification and reflection activities while evaluating rather than assuming their effects on engagement.
                            
                            
                              Policymakers should develop equity‐oriented strategies that support the digital and cultural integration of disadvantaged student groups.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: Catching the spark: The role of electrodermal activity in understanding teacher enthusiasm and students' lesson enjoyment
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Process‐oriented approaches are needed to understand the temporality and dynamics of teacher–student interactions in higher education classrooms. In this study, we follow a complexity science approach, based on non‐linear intra‐ and inter‐personal physiology methods, to explore the physiology of teacher–student interactions. In particular, we examine the relationship between higher education students' course interest, electrodermal activity (EDA, as an indicator of physiological arousal), perceived teacher enthusiasm in the classroom and lesson enjoyment. Ten higher education teachers and 42 of their students voluntarily participated in this study. Self‐reported measures were applied to assess students' course interest (pre), perceived teacher enthusiasm (post) and lesson enjoyment (post) in authentic higher education lectures. Teachers' and students' EDA was sampled at 2 kHz using Bionomadix mobile sensors during the lectures. Auto‐ and cross‐recurrence quantification analyses were applied to understand the temporal structures of students' individual EDA patterns and their physiological synchrony with their teachers. At the individual level, entropy of students' EDA predicted their perceived teacher enthusiasm and lesson enjoyment beyond course interest. At the physiological synchrony level, course interest was the only predictor of students' perceived teacher enthusiasm and lesson enjoyment. Moreover, our findings showed that the relationships between course interest and the structure of EDA patterns differ between individual and physiological synchrony levels. These results provide valuable insight into understanding interactions between teachers and students from a complexity science perspective.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic?
                          
                            
                              Control value theory (CVT) defines academic emotions in terms of the two dimensions of valence (positive or negative) and arousal (activating or deactivating).
                            
                            
                              Enjoyment is considered a positive activating emotion that is central to effective teaching and learning.
                            
                            
                              Emotions in the classroom are dynamically co‐constructed through social interactions among teachers and students.
                            
                            
                              While valence is inherently subjective, objective physiological measures like electrodermal activity (EDA) are increasingly utilised to understand the arousal dimension of emotions and the dynamics of emotional contagion between teachers and students.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds?
                          
                            
                              Observing EDA of higher education students during authentic lectures can provide valuable insights into their perceived teacher enthusiasm and lesson enjoyment.
                            
                            
                              Exploring the temporal structures of EDA through nonlinear methods might help understand the emergence of students' lesson enjoyment in a bottom‐up manner.
                            
                            
                              Studying temporal structures of EDA at intra‐ and interpersonal levels (i.e. teacher–student physiological synchrony) can provide a multilayered perspective on the relationship between students' course interest, perceived teacher enthusiasm and lesson enjoyment.
                            
                            
                              At the intra‐personal level, students' course interest and their EDA entropy both predict perceived teacher enthusiasm and lesson enjoyment.
                            
                            
                              At the inter‐personal level, teacher–student physiological synchrony occurs above chance level. Furthermore, physiological synchrony is associated with students' course interest. However, it does not predict perceived teacher enthusiasm or lesson enjoyment beyond the influence of course interest.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              Teachers and learning designers can focus on fostering high course interest among learners at the beginning of their courses to facilitate positive relational dynamics with the students.
                            
                            
                              Moving educational research towards non‐linear approaches can provide more nuanced insights into how students' and teachers' emotions evolve in higher education classrooms.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: Connecting the dots to understand complex systems in education: A systematic review of psychological networks
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Psychological networks have emerged as a robust methodology for examining complex systems. Although their use has become increasingly important in psychology and behavioural research, they remain underutilized in the field of educational research. Consequently, limited information is available regarding their adoption and the techniques employed to investigate various educational dimensions. To address this research gap, this systematic review study analysed 43 studies to examine the application of psychological networks in education, focusing on their methodologies and the educational objectives or phenomena explored. The findings revealed that psychological networks have been used to investigate six primary educational dimensions: cognitive, psychological, motivational, sociological and cultural, behavioural and knowledge and performance. Additionally, we identified several challenges associated with this approach, including the complexity of network interpretation, methodological complexity and integrity.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Psychological networks are frequently used in psychology.
                            
                            
                              The use of psychological networks in education is still in its infancy.
                            
                            
                              Limited information exists on how psychological networks are applied in education and for which purposes.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study conducts a systematic review to provide an in‐depth understanding of psychological networks in education.
                            
                            
                              It reveals that psychological networks are mostly applied in language learning.
                            
                            
                              Psychological networks are capable of modelling six educational dimensions, namely cognitive, psychological, motivational, sociological and cultural, behavioural and knowledge and performance.
                            
                            
                              Psychological networks in education rely on several core models, including Gaussian Graphical Model, Mixed Graphical Model, Markov Random Field, Bayesian Gaussian graphical model and Vector Autoregression.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              This study identifies several different types of challenges, including complexity of network interpretation, methodological complexity and integrity.
                            
                            
                              Practitioners should rely more on the triangulation method of data to provide more insights that could be generalized when using psychological networks in education.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Many hands make light work? Individual and collaborative interaction with a
                    <scp>GenAI</scp>
                    ‐powered multi‐agent system: Effects on learning performance and critical thinking
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has made fostering learners' critical thinking an increasingly pressing educational challenge. While single‐agent GenAI applications are prone to limited perspective diversity and echo‐chamber effects, multi‐agent systems (MAS) offer a promising alternative by enabling multi‐perspective interactions. Meanwhile, the pedagogical potential of collaborative human–GenAI interaction, particularly when peers jointly engage with MAS to promote epistemic diversity, remains underexplored. Moreover, little is known about how critical thinking unfolds within such interactions at a process‐oriented level. This study investigates how different configurations of peer collaboration and GenAI‐powered multi‐agent support are associated with learning performance, critical thinking awareness and interaction processes. A quasi‐experimental study was conducted with 87 undergraduate students enrolled in an instructional design course. Participants were assigned to a peer collaboration condition without AI support, an individual human–MAS interaction condition or a collaborative human–MAS interaction condition. Learning performance was assessed using knowledge tests and design projects, critical thinking awareness was measured via a questionnaire and critical thinking processes were examined through lag sequential analysis and epistemic network analysis. The results indicate that collaborative interaction with the MAS corresponded to higher project performance, whereas individual interaction was associated with greater gains in critical thinking awareness. Process analyses further suggest distinct cognitive trajectories across configurations, with individual interaction characterised by more focused analytical–evaluative processing and collaborative interaction involving more distributed and integrative reasoning. These findings highlight the importance of aligning MAS design with appropriate human–AI collaboration configurations to better facilitate critical thinking in GenAI‐supported learning environments.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            
                              Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being incorporated into educational settings, raising ongoing interest in how AI‐supported learning environments can engage learners in higher‐order cognitive processes, including critical thinking.
                            
                            
                              Many existing AI‐supported learning environments rely on single‐agent systems, which may unintentionally encourage answer‐seeking behaviours and reinforce echo‐chamber effects.
                            
                            
                              Multi‐agent systems (MAS) provide role‐differentiated support and exposure to diverse perspectives, and have been suggested as a promising approach for supporting higher‐order thinking in learning.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            
                              By developing a GenAI‐supported multi‐agent system, this study empirically compares learning outcomes across peer collaboration without AI support, individual interaction with the MAS, and collaborative interaction with the MAS, showing that individual interaction is linked to higher critical thinking awareness gains, whereas collaborative interaction corresponds to stronger performance on complex design‐oriented tasks.
                            
                            
                              Through the integration of lag sequential analysis and epistemic network analysis, the study reveals how overt interaction behaviours and implicit cognitive structures jointly reflect critical thinking processes in multi‐agent learning environments.
                            
                            
                              The findings provide initial process‐level insights suggesting that multi‐agent systems may function not merely as information providers, but as reflective and socially mediating supports that facilitate how learners regulate, negotiate and integrate ideas during learning.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            
                              Educators can deliberately align human–GenAI interaction configurations with specific instructional goals, as individual interaction with a multi‐agent system may be more conducive to learners' critical thinking awareness, and collaborative interaction may be better suited for complex design and problem‐solving tasks.
                            
                            
                              Instructional designers are encouraged to embed explicit reflective checkpoints or targeted critical thinking scaffolds within collaborative human–MAS interaction settings to mitigate reduced opportunities for individual metacognitive monitoring.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly framed as a catalyst for deeper learning rather than simple automation. This design-based study investigated how personalised GPT agents were used as cognitive partners by pre-service teachers in an undergraduate Initial Teacher Education course in Digital Technologies within a Bachelor of Education (Secondary) programme. Drawing on distributed cognition, constructivism, cognitive load theory, and critical AI literacy, the intervention embedded personalised GPT agents within a university Canvas Learning Management System. Fourteen students configured and used agents aligned to curriculum goals, teaching contexts, pedagogical preferences, and weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks. Data included approximately 7,000 AI interactions, reflective journals, assessed lesson and assessment artefacts, and tutorial-group discussions. A hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis identified four recurrent functions in students’ use of the agents: conceptual tutor, co-designer, reflective mirror, and cognitive challenger. Across data sources, students reported clearer conceptual support, iterative planning, and reflective prompting, alongside risks of over-reliance, factual drift, and culturally narrow exemplars. The study contributes a context-specific model for LMS-integrated generative AI that foregrounds partnership, personalisation, judgement, and ethical reflexivity. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study was small-scale, single-site, and partly reliant on self-reported reflection.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  This study examines post-intervention self-reported outcomes associated with a short intervention designed to introduce coding, educational robotics, and introductory concepts of machine learning into initial teacher education for Primary Education. The proposal is grounded in Papert’s principles and the Creative and Computational Problem Solving model, combining active learning methodologies with accessible technologies. A quasi-experimental design with a non-equivalent control group was employed. A total of 144 first-year students from three Spanish universities participated (105 in the experimental group and 39 in the control group). The intervention consisted of a two-hour workshop with hands-on stations and technological challenges, designed as a feasible microintervention within regular teacher education contexts. Assessment was carried out through an ad hoc questionnaire focused on three dimensions: knowledge of programming and machine learning, block-based programming and game engines, and active learning, all assessed through self-reported perceptions. The results showed statistically significant post-intervention differences in favor of the experimental group, with a small effect size for knowledge of programming and machine learning and large effect sizes for block-based programming and game engines and active learning. Item-level analyses revealed that favorable overall perceptions coexisted with lower self-reported familiarity in specific technical areas, particularly machine learning, prior experience with block-based programming, and programming in game engines. Three exploratory response profiles were also identified: reluctant, intermediate, and enthusiastic. The findings suggest that well-structured microinterventions may support higher self-reported knowledge of programming and machine learning, greater familiarity with block-based programming and game engines, and more positive perceptions of active learning in teacher education.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
The Nexus of Innovation: Technological, Organizational, and Environmental Influences on
                    <scp>VR</scp>
                    Adoption in Libraries
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Virtual reality (VR) technology offers immersive, interactive, and engaging educational experiences. It can significantly improve how well students understand and retain their learning for complex subjects.
                  
                  
                    Purpose
                    This study explores the nexus of technological, organizational, and environmental factors influencing the readiness to adopt and the adoption of VR in academic libraries.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    Drawing on the Technological‐Organizational‐Environmental model as the theoretical foundation, data were collected from 232 Chinese Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) using the stratified random sampling method and analysed using Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modelling.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Factors from all three categories, including perceived benefits, monetary resources, information and communication technology infrastructure, HEIs support, and market dynamics, had significant positive effects on VR technology readiness towards its adoption, whereas perceived complexity had a negative effect. Moreover, VR technology readiness was a significant mediator in the relationships between the factors and VR technology adoption. Control variables, including HEIs ranking and number of students, and the Importance‐Performance Map yielded mixed results.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    This study is novel as it extends the investigation of VR adoption, which has been predominantly explored in commercial and industrial contexts, to the underexplored setting of academic libraries, particularly within the Chinese context. Additionally, by integrating VR technology readiness as a mediating variable, this study offers unique insights into technology adoption in academic libraries, thereby addressing critical research gaps. The findings can aid HEIs administrators, policy makers, and educators in planning, assessing, and implementing VR‐based technologies, enabling them to gain a more comprehensive understanding of users' satisfaction and promote the sustained use of advanced VR systems.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
The Influence of the Role of Peer Presence on Game‐Based Chemistry Learning: Evidence From
                    <scp>EEG</scp>
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Game‐based learning (GBL) has become an important way to innovate chemistry teaching. However, it is still unclear how different peer roles in GBL shape learners' learning outcomes and cognitive processes.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    The study examined how different peer roles (individual vs. collaborators vs. competitors) influence learners' outcomes in game‐based chemistry learning. It also examined differences in theta and alpha power across these conditions.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    The study employed a between‐subjects design with 69 ninth‐grade students from a secondary school in China who had not yet learned the target chemical concepts. Students were randomly assigned to individual, collaborative or competitive learning. Outcome measurement included immediate and delayed testing, motivation, cognitive load, interest and electroencephalography (EEG)‐based alpha and theta power.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Both the collaborative and competitive conditions showed higher learning performance and interest than the individual condition. The collaborative condition also showed higher motivation than both the competitive and individual conditions and higher cognitive load than the individual condition. EEG analyses showed that the collaborative condition elicited higher theta and alpha power than the individual condition across both phases, although differences from the competitive condition were not consistently significant. These patterns may reflect greater demands on cognitive control and selective processing during collaborative learning.
                  
                  
                    Implications
                    The findings highlight the value of collaborative peer roles in game‐based chemistry learning. Teachers may consider incorporating structured collaborative activities to promote students' engagement and cognitive involvement. The findings also suggest that different peer roles may serve distinct motivational functions, which may inform the design of GBL activities.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Writing Motivation and Self‐Efficacy in
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐Chatbot‐Supported
                    <scp>EFL</scp>
                    Writing: Exploratory Insights Across Proficiency Levels
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Writing motivation and self‐efficacy are critical factors of success in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts, yet they are frequently undermined by learner anxiety and limited teacher feedback. While artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots offer potential for adaptive writing support, limited research has examined these affective constructs in parallel across learner proficiency levels.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study investigated changes in intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy among high school EFL learners at higher‐ and lower‐proficiency levels following chatbot‐supported writing and examined whether these changes differed across proficiency levels.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    Using an exploratory mixed‐methods design, the study involved 47 Vietnamese high school students divided into higher‐ and lower‐proficiency level groups. Over the 11‐week study, participants completed 8 weeks of AI‐supported writing activities using a chatbot designed in accordance with principles of Self‐Determination Theory, Self‐Regulated Learning Theory and Self‐Efficacy Theory. Changes in intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy were examined using pre‐ and post‐questionnaires and semi‐structured interviews.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    The quantitative findings revealed that intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy increased over time in both proficiency groups, with no significant differences in the magnitude of change between higher‐ and lower‐proficiency learners. This suggests that the affective changes observed during AI‐supported writing were not confined to one proficiency group. The qualitative findings indicated that learners linked their positive experiences to reduced anxiety, clearer guidance, and supportive interaction, although the types of support they valued differed by proficiency level. Overall, the findings suggest that when positioned as a supportive writing partner rather than an answer generator, AI chatbot feedback may be associated with positive motivational and self‐efficacy development in mixed‐ability EFL writing classrooms.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Desktop Virtual Reality for Public First‐Aid Training: Effects on Cognitive Load and Learning Outcomes
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Public first‐aid education must help learners apply procedural knowledge in emergencies, yet conventional instruction offers limited contextualized practice. Desktop virtual reality (DVR) can provide interactive, scenario‐based learning, but evidence regarding its effects on cognitive load and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) knowledge is inconclusive.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    Our study compared DVR‐based and video‐based CPR instruction in terms of learners' cognitive load and performance on CPR knowledge.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      Eighty‐four university students were randomly allocated to DVR or video instruction. Complete‐case analyses included 64 participants (32 per condition) with valid cognitive‐load, pre‐test and post‐test data. Between‐group differences were examined using two‐sided independent‐samples
                      t
                      ‐tests and Mann–Whitney
                      U
                      tests; interviews with six DVR participants were analysed deductively to contextualize their experiences.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    
                      The DVR group reported lower overall cognitive load (
                      p
                       = 0.010) and lower scores on both prespecified cognitive load dimensions, cognitive behavioural assessment (
                      p
                       = 0.033) and cognitive efficiency assessment (
                      p
                       = 0.015), than the video group. At post‐test, DVR participants performed better on the four‐item CPR detail set (
                      p
                       = 0.038), while the groups did not differ on basic items. The tested DVR condition, which combined signal guidance, spatial visualization, multisensory stimulation, self‐paced progression, scenario simulation and prompt feedback, was associated with lower reported cognitive load and better performance on the CPR detail knowledge than video instruction, while performance on the basic knowledge did not differ. These findings support the use of DVR as a structured supplement to CPR instruction, enabling learners to rehearse spatial and procedural relations at their own pace and receive prompt feedback. They also suggest that designers should evaluate guidance, navigation, feedback and scenario features as an integrated instructional configuration.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: How Generative AI-Assisted Formative Feedback Is Appraised and Implemented in Online Collaborative Learning
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants (
                    n
                    = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Socratic, Artifact-Gated Generative AI Scaffolding in a 6E Inquiry Unit: A Clustered Quasi-Experiment in Elementary Students’ Computational Thinking
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Open-ended computational thinking (CT) inquiry challenges one teacher to support learners progressing at different rates. This clustered quasi-experiment evaluated TALPer, a generative-AI tutor providing student-initiated, artifact-contingent Socratic prompts during a six-lesson 6E unit. Ten intact Grade 3 classes in Taiwan (N = 229) completed the same curriculum, tasks, teacher, platform, and instructional time. Conditions differed in a bundled scaffolding configuration involving source, delivery modality, initiation, privacy, and artifact requirements. A two-level model controlling for pretest CT estimated an adjusted posttest difference favoring TALPer (
                    B
                    = 4.05,
                    SE
                    = 1.58, Wald 95% CI [0.94, 7.15],
                    p
                    = .011; sensitivity
                    p
                    = .034; Hedges’
                    g
                    = 0.52). Class-clustered analyses found no Holm-adjusted difference on any Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscale; Perceived Choice had the largest positive estimate (
                    B
                    = 0.27, cluster-adjusted
                    SE
                    = 0.12, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.55],
                    p
                    = .061, pHolm = .306; Hedges’
                    g
                    = 0.38). The Condition × Pretest interaction was nonsignificant (
                    B
                    = −0.109,
                    SE
                    = 0.125, 95% CI [-0.354, 0.137],
                    p
                    = .385). Descriptive coding of 101 matched responses showed different distributions of expected and planned AI-use orientations; no inferential transition test was conducted. Findings provide preliminary evidence concerning the bundled intervention but do not isolate component contributions.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: From Prompting to Scaffolding: Divergent Human–AI Interaction Pathways of Pre-Service Teachers in Multi-Agent Micro-Teaching Simulation (MAMS)
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Traditional micro-teaching offers limited opportunities for pre-service teachers to rehearse classroom contingencies in repeatable, standardized ways. This study developed a multi-agent micro-teaching simulation (MAMS), informed by professional noticing, to expand practice-based learning opportunities for pre-service mathematics teachers (PSTs). MAMS integrates differentiated virtual students, standardized challenge events, and Dean Agent prompts to create comparable classroom contingencies. Sixty-four PSTs completed two simulated micro-teaching sessions and were analytically classified into higher and lower baseline mathematics pedagogical content knowledge (MPCK) profiles. Outcomes included teacher self-efficacy, MPCK performance, and Community of Inquiry presence; interaction logs were analyzed using event-anchored lag sequential analysis. Under the standardized MAMS condition, outcome analyses showed observed pre–post changes and modest baseline-adjusted profile differences. The higher baseline MPCK profile showed stronger MPCK response-strategy performance and higher Teaching Presence; Social and Cognitive Presence showed no reliable profile differences. Log analyses revealed divergent feedback-to-action pathways: higher baseline MPCK PSTs more often moved from Dean Agent prompts to diagnostic questioning and scaffolding, followed by substantive student responses, whereas lower baseline MPCK PSTs more often shifted to direct instruction or process regulation, followed by continued low participation. These findings suggest a need for prior-knowledge-responsive scaffolding in AI-supported teacher education.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: From Local to Global: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Validation of the SAGAI Scale for Measuring Student Attitudes Toward Generative AI
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming an increasingly visible component of higher education, raising the need for theoretically grounded instruments that can capture how students perceive and engage with these technologies. This study aims to adapt the Scale for Attitudes toward Generative Artificial Intelligence (SAGAI), originally developed in Turkish, into English and to examine its psychometric properties within a different linguistic context. The study was conducted with 350 higher education students enrolled at a UK-based open and distance learning institution. A systematic cross-cultural adaptation process was followed, including translation, back-translation, expert review, and pilot testing. Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to examine the structural validity of the scale. The findings supported a four-factor structure—usefulness, anxiety, expectancy, and competency—consistent with the original model, with acceptable to strong model fit indices after minor modifications, resulting in a 22-item version. Reliability analyses indicated high internal consistency across all dimensions. Comparative analyses examined differences between the Turkish and English samples at both total and dimensional levels. Turkish participants reported higher levels of usefulness, expectancy, and anxiety, whereas English participants demonstrated higher perceived competency. Additional analyses within the UK sample indicated that prior experience with GenAI was strongly associated with attitudinal differences, pointing to the role of usage in shaping how these technologies are evaluated. The findings indicate that the underlying structure of attitudes toward GenAI remains stable across linguistic contexts, while the intensity and balance of these dimensions vary depending on contextual and experiential factors. The coexistence of positive expectations and concerns suggests that student attitudes toward GenAI are inherently multidimensional rather than uniformly positive or negative. The study provides evidence that SAGAI is a valid and reliable instrument for use in English-speaking contexts and offers a structured framework for examining student attitudes toward GenAI in cross-cultural research. The results also underline the importance of considering both context and experience when interpreting how students engage with emerging technologies.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: A Meta-Analysis of Intelligent Homework Systems (IHS): Effects on Academic Performance and the Role of Functional Features
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Research on Intelligent Homework Systems (IHS) has expanded with the increasing integration of automated assessment, feedback, and adaptive support into homework environments. However, existing studies have reported mixed effects on academic performance, and it remains unclear whether variations in learner, instructional, and functional characteristics contribute to this heterogeneity. This study examined the overall effect of IHS on learners’ academic performance and the moderating roles of learner, instructional, and IHS functional characteristics. Thirty-seven experimental and quasi-experimental studies published between 1995 and 2025 were included, yielding 38 effect sizes from 17,682 learners across 15 countries or regions. Using a random-effects model, we found a statistically significant small-to-moderate positive effect of IHS on academic performance (Hedges’ g = .419, 95% CI [.298, .541],
                    p
                    < .001). Moderator analyses showed that scoring mechanism, granularity of diagnosis, and level of feedback elaboration significantly moderated the effects of IHS, whereas learning domain, cultural background, grade level, degree of adaptivity, and mastery criterion did not. The medium level of granularity of diagnosis and the medium level of feedback elaboration showed the largest pooled effects. The findings suggest that IHS effectiveness depends not merely on the presence of intelligent functions, but on how instructional support is configured.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: What counts as digital play? Irish early childhood educators’ beliefs and practice tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly embedded in young children’s lives, yet uncertainty remains regarding their role in early childhood education and care (ECEC). This study explores Irish early years educators’ beliefs and perceptions concerning digital play, employing Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological framework to examine how policy, parental expectations and professional identity interact to shape children’s learning opportunities. Semi-structured interviews with 10 educators identified five themes: developmentalist beliefs prioritising ‘natural’ play, cautious openness to digital tools, professional identity and ethical tensions, perceptions of children and families and concerns about policy directives. Findings reveal a persistent policy–practice gap, where limited professional development and unclear guidance leave educators uncertain about how to define and implement quality digital play. The study emphasises that educators’ attitudes are closely associated with the extent and quality of children’s digital engagement, highlighting the need for sustained professional development and strengthened mesosystemic communication across home, school and policy contexts. Implications include the creation of context-sensitive frameworks that integrate digital and traditional play while supporting children’s holistic development. This study demonstrates that educators’ definitions of digital play are shaped by the interaction of professional identity, policy ambiguity, family expectations and resource conditions, offering new insight into the conditions that constrain digital play in Irish early years settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Teachers’ professional learning and development experiences in Chinese kindergartens: Opportunities and tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Professional learning and development (PLD) activities for Chinese kindergarten teachers have introduced imported knowledge to promote teaching and learning. Much PLD provision is led by leaders and experts rather than teachers. To understand the educational beliefs and power differences that surface among teachers, leaders and experts during PLD sessions and how teachers navigate this complex terrain, this paper presents a post-intentional phenomenological study involving seven participants from two Chinese early childhood settings. Data collection included semi-structured interviews, observations of PLD meetings and videos of teachers’ implementation of PLD ideas. Educational policies, PLD materials, and the researcher’s reflexive journal were also used for analysis. Analysis involved a line-by-line reading process where theoretical concepts, data and researcher reflexivity interacted. The findings reveal that teachers experienced tensions in relation to formal PLD sessions. These tensions stemmed from established values and hierarchical constraints that limited their joint reflection and actions. Our analysis, framed by the concepts of relational agency and in-between spaces, shows how teachers navigated these tensions. Despite these constraints, the teachers responded by creating opportunities for collaborative learning. They sought out informal situations where they had the flexibility to develop shared knowledge. We argue that Chinese teachers’ PLD can occur within and across such tensions and opportunities. These informal situations empowered teachers to enact relational agency by aligning their expertise to make PLD decisions. This process eased tensions and created space for collaborative learning. The study concludes that valuing these informal, teacher-initiated spaces is crucial for moving beyond top-down knowledge transmission and fostering sustainable professional growth in hierarchical educational contexts. Ultimately, by empowering teachers as collaborative and adaptable professionals, this model of PLD offers new insights into enhancing the professional environments that shape teaching practice and young children’s learning.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Parent–school mobile communication in preschool: A qualitative study in Mexico
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: School-family communication in early childhood is increasingly mediated by mobile applications, yet important questions remain about what counts as high-quality content, how schools allocate topics between digital and face-to-face channels, and what costs these practices impose on teachers. This qualitative study examines how a mobile application shapes day-to-day parent-school communication in a Mexican preschool. Semi-structured interviews with four teachers and three mothers, combined with field observation, were thematically analyzed. The app supported timely and consistent exchanges about classroom life. Families valued brief, concrete descriptions of children’s socio-emotional participation, peer interactions, and strategies practiced, along with simple suggestions for follow-up at home. However, participants identified a depth gap when messages focused mainly on logistics, and teachers reported a workload tension between the burden of exhaustive daily reporting and the sense of security it provides to parents. A hybrid model of communication was preferred: routine updates and nonurgent questions were handled in the app, while complex, evaluative, or sensitive topics were addressed in planned one-to-one meetings. Reported short-term gains were primarily psychosocial, including higher trust and a closer working relationship between teachers and families. Findings support a shift from tool adoption to the quality of communicative practice in early childhood settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Promoting social skills and friendships in early childhood education: A case study of four children’s trajectories to inclusion
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper reports on the changes reported on the social relations and skills of four children after the implementation of ProFriend (Promoting Friendship) in an early childhood education (ECE) setting. ProFriend is a programme developed considering the inclusive ECE principles by targeting all children’s access and participation and looking beyond imposed labels. The data of the study included friendship nominations, observations, children’s drawings, teachers’ interviews and research diary. The findings shed light on four children’s trajectories who faced challenges in forming friendships and whose individual characteristics (speech and language impairments and socio-emotional difficulties) were seen by teachers as barriers to their social development. The discussion focuses on how children’s exclusion can be minimised by enriching ECE curricula with some elements guiding teachers on how to approach the development of social skills and friendships in a meaningful and inclusive way.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: The impact of active transitions on preschool students’ self-regulation
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Early childhood education plays a pivotal role in fostering the holistic development of young learners through age-appropriate activities and interactions that support physical, social, emotional and cognitive growth. This study explored the relationship between active transitions in an early childhood education classroom and observable behaviour indicators of self-regulation in preschoolers, with a specific focus on the integration of yoga during transitional times. The objective was to investigate the impact of incorporating yoga on student self-regulation during large group literacy, as perceived by the preschool teacher. The research employed a collaborative action research design, engaging a preschool teacher in a reflective and systematic approach to improve classroom practices. Findings indicated that the integration of yoga, when including both challenging and sedentary poses, was associated with reductions in teacher-observed off-task behaviour during large group literacy, suggesting a possible positive influence on behaviour self-regulation. Results indicated that active transitions may support overall classroom management, increased instructional time and contributed to a comprehensive understanding of the effects of physical activity on young learners.

keyword_papers.title: AI intelligence within Teaching: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Large Language Model Education Agents in K-12 Education
keyword_papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping K–12 education by enabling adaptive and pedagogically responsive learning environments. This study presents a multidimensional evaluation of LLM-based learning agents using the Educational–Technical–Behavioural (ETB) Framework to assess pedagogical quality, technical reliability, and behavioural intelligence. ScienceSpark AI, a curriculum-aligned platform for the NSW Science 7–10 syllabus, was tested with Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3, ChatGPT-5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 within a unified agentic architecture. Using synthetic benchmarking, sandboxed simulations, and teacher-in-the-loop validation, the study found all models achieved strong curriculum alignment, factual accuracy, and multimodal feedback capability. Gemini 3 delivered the best technical performance, showing the lowest latency in conversation (~10s) and resource generation (~5.7s), while maintaining the high educational fidelity of Gemini 2.5 Pro. ChatGPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 excelled in conversational fluency and creative resource generation. Overall, the findings demonstrate that when grounded in transparent architecture and curriculum-driven design, LLM agents can provide both technical efficiency and equitable instructional support. The ETB Framework offers a replicable approach for evaluating and governing AI in education.
keyword_papers.venue: 2025 International Conference on Computational Engineering, Sensing Technology and Management (ICCETM)

keyword_papers.title: A systematic literature review to implement large language model in higher education: issues and solutions
keyword_papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven Chatbots, especially large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4, represent significant progress in digital education. These models excel in mimicking human-like text and transforming learning and teaching methods. This study examines the development, application, and impact of LLMs in education. It highlights their role in automating instructional tasks and promoting personalized learning experiences. Despite integration concerns and ethical debates, LLMs showcase the potential of AI to improve educational practices. Our research concludes that LLMs offer transformative opportunities for education. However, their incorporation requires careful ethical considerations, data privacy measures, and a balance between human educators and AI technologies. The findings suggest strategies for integrating LLMs into educational frameworks to enhance learning outcomes while preserving educational integrity.

keyword_papers.title: Developing Effective Frameworks for Large Language Model–Based Medical Chatbots: Insights From Radiotherapy Education With ChatGPT
keyword_papers.abstract: This Viewpoint proposes a robust framework for developing a medical chatbot dedicated to radiotherapy education, emphasizing accuracy, reliability, privacy, ethics, and future innovations. By analyzing existing research, the framework evaluates chatbot performance and identifies challenges such as content accuracy, bias, and system integration. The findings highlight opportunities for advancements in natural language processing, personalized learning, and immersive technologies. When designed with a focus on ethical standards and reliability, large language model–based chatbots could significantly impact radiotherapy education and health care delivery, positioning them as valuable tools for future developments in medical education globally.

keyword_papers.title: Advancing AI in Higher Education: A Comparative Study of Large Language Model-Based Agents for Exam Question Generation, Improvement, and Evaluation
keyword_papers.abstract: The transformative capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are reshaping educational assessment and question design in higher education. This study proposes a systematic framework for leveraging LLMs to enhance question-centric tasks: aligning exam questions with course objectives, improving clarity and difficulty, and generating new items guided by learning goals. The research spans four university courses—two theory-focused and two application-focused—covering diverse cognitive levels according to Bloom’s taxonomy. A balanced dataset ensures representation of question categories and structures. Three LLM-based agents—VectorRAG, VectorGraphRAG, and a fine-tuned LLM—are developed and evaluated against a meta-evaluator, supervised by human experts, to assess alignment accuracy and explanation quality. Robust analytical methods, including mixed-effects modeling, yield actionable insights for integrating generative AI into university assessment processes. Beyond exam-specific applications, this methodology provides a foundational approach for the broader adoption of AI in post-secondary education, emphasizing fairness, contextual relevance, and collaboration. The findings offer a comprehensive framework for aligning AI-generated content with learning objectives, detailing effective integration strategies, and addressing challenges such as bias and contextual limitations. Overall, this work underscores the potential of generative AI to enhance educational assessment while identifying pathways for responsible implementation.

keyword_papers.title: Embracing the Future of Medical Education With Large Language Model–Based Virtual Patients: Scoping Review
keyword_papers.abstract: Background In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have experienced rapid development. LLM-based virtual patients have begun to gain attention, offering new opportunities for simulations in medical education. Objective This study aims to systematically analyze the current applications, research trends, and challenges of LLM-based virtual patients in medical education and to explore potential future directions for development. Methods This study adheres to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five databases (Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Embase, and Scopus) were searched from January 1, 2018, to June 24, 2025, to identify studies related to the application of LLM-based virtual patients in medical education. A comprehensive analysis of LLM-based virtual patients from research design to application and evaluation was conducted. Results A total of 28 studies were included in this scoping review. Analysis revealed that 92.9% (26/28) of the studies were published in the past 2 years, indicating that LLM-based virtual patient research is still in its early stages. The research primarily focuses on medical training and spans a wide range of medical disciplines. When using LLMs, advanced technologies such as social robots, virtual reality, and mixed reality are used to present LLM-based virtual patients. Combining these technologies with various supplementary tools enhances the realism of LLM-based virtual patients and improves user interaction. The evaluation of LLM-based virtual patients mainly emphasizes user experience. However, evaluation methods lack standardization, and only 13% (3/23) of studies used validated tools in assessing LLM-based virtual patients, while only 21.7% (5/23) of studies objectively measured learning outcomes facilitated by LLM-based virtual patients. All included studies expressed a positive attitude toward LLM-based virtual patients; however, they overlook privacy and security considerations in practical applications. Conclusions LLM-based virtual patients hold significant innovation potential in medical education and are still in the early stages of development. They are primarily applied in medical training and show promise in communication skills training, although they cannot replace real-world interactions. Moreover, the heterogeneity of research designs, the absence of nonverbal cues in interactions, and concerns regarding privacy and security limit their broader implementation. Future research should focus on improving the reliability, realism, safety, and scientific efficacy of LLM-based virtual patients. keyword_papers.title: Effectiveness of Robot-Mediated Learning in Fostering Children’s Social and Cognitive Development
keyword_papers.abstract: Engaging with social robots has been recognized as potentially beneficial for children facing social communication challenges, especially in developing skills such as joint attention. This systematic review examines the effectiveness of robot-mediated learning in enhancing children’s cognitive abilities, emotional resilience, and self-confidence, based on an analysis of research conducted between 2018 and 2025. While social robots show promise in delivering personalized and engaging educational experiences, challenges such as emotional dependence, accessibility, and ethical concerns persist. The review concludes that further research, particularly longitudinal studies and cross-cultural comparisons, is necessary to fully understand the long-term impacts of robot-mediated learning on children’s cognitive and social development. It explores the application of robotic technology in relation to children’s educational progress across different age groups. The review includes studies of various types, such as experimental, non-experimental, and research articles, covering diverse research fields, robots, contexts of use, target audiences, and outcomes. The findings highlight the growing potential of social robots to support children’s cognitive development by providing interactive and stimulating learning experiences. This review offers valuable insights for researchers and designers aiming to improve robotic interventions and tailor them to meet diverse developmental needs and educational settings.

keyword_papers.title: IMPACT OF TECHNOLOGY ON SOCIAL AND COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT IN CHILDREN
keyword_papers.abstract:
Technology has inuenced children's social and cognitive development in recent years. This article explores both the
positive and negative impacts of technology on children's social and cognitive development. On the one hand, technology
can provide children with the opportunity to learn and engage in activities that may not be available in their home environment. This can lead to
increased condence and improved problem-solving skills. On the other hand, technology can lead to a decrease in physical activity, an increase in
feelings of isolation and loneliness, an over-dependence on technology, and a decrease in creativity and problem-solving skills. The article also
discusses technology's potential implications on children's social and cognitive development. It looks at how technology can both positively and
negatively affect children's development. It also looks at how it can be used to help them grow and develop healthily. Ultimately, this article
provides insight into the impact of technology on children's social and cognitive development and the potential implications of technology on
their lives

keyword_papers.title: Effects of Robotics Education on Young Children’s Cognitive Development: a Pilot Study with Eye-Tracking
keyword_papers.abstract: The emerging field of robotics education (RE) is a new and rapidly growing subject area worldwide. It may provide a playful and novel learning environment for children to engage with all aspects of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning. The purpose of this research is to examine how robotics learning activities may affect the cognitive abilities and cognitive processes of 6–8 years old children. The study adopted the mixed methods approach with a repeated measures design; three waves of data collection over 6 months, including quantitative data obtained from cognitive assessments and eye-tracking, and qualitative data from the interviews. A total of 31 children were recruited from an afterschool robotics program. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first RE research that used a combination of eye-tracking, cognitive assessments, and interviews for examining the effect of RE on children. Using linear growth models, the results of cognitive assessments showed that children’s visuospatial working memory as well as logical and abstract reasoning skills improved over time. The interview data were analyzed by a thematic analysis. The results revealed that children perceived RE activities as game play, which made children more engaged in their study; parents found their children to be more focused on activities comparing to six months ago. Additionally, the visualization of the eye-tracking data suggested that children became more focused on RE activities and got faster to process the information across six months in general, which echoed the findings in assessments and interviews. Our findings may help educators and policymakers better understand the benefits of RE for young children.
keyword_papers.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology

keyword_papers.title: The Impact of Technology on Cognitive Development in Early Childhood
keyword_papers.abstract: Technology integration into everyday life is deeper than ever in this age of fast technological innovation. This is particularly true for young children exposed to numerous digital instruments from an early age. Such integration has sparked concerns about how technology may affect young childrens cognitive growth, a crucial time when mental capacities like thinking, reasoning, and understanding are still developing. Recognizing the significance of this conversation, the background for this study is the growing anxiety among parents, teachers, and lawmakers over the influence of technology on childrens brains. This study uses a literature review methodology to examine previously published academic studies to understand the complex connection between technology and cognitive development. It aims to grasp both the rewarding possibilities and the dangers it offers. The conclusion summarizes the results and highlights methods for maximizing technologys positive effects while minimizing its possible drawbacks, providing a comprehensive understanding of the subject.
keyword_papers.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media

keyword_papers.title: The Use of Technology in the Cognitive Development of Early Children
keyword_papers.abstract: This study was conducted to analyze how the effect of gadget use in early childhood on children's cognitive development. This research is a qualitative descriptive study. the source of the data used is the result of observations of children and parents regarding the use of gadgets in children's cognitive development at Kindergarten Risanti I, West Jakarta. The research result show use of gadgets in children can improve cognitive development of children. through gadgets, children can learn independently about language or mathematics. children's learning through gadgets must be under the supervision of parents. children should not be allowed to use gadgets as they wish. The positive impact of using gadgets on children, consisting of: Improved cognitive skills, More fun for kids, and Educating young ones. The negative impact of using gadgets on children, consisting of: Learning problems, Anxiety, Lazy thinking, Decreased concentration, and hyperactivity.

keyword_papers.title: Autism Detection in Children: Integrating Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing in Narrative Analysis
keyword_papers.abstract: Despite the consensus that early identification leads to better outcomes for individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), recent research reveals that the average age of diagnosis in the Greek population is approximately six years. However, this age of diagnosis is delayed by an additional two years for families from lower-income or minority backgrounds. These disparities result in adverse impacts on intervention outcomes, which are further burdened by the often time-consuming and labor-intensive language assessments for children with ASD. There is a crucial need for tools that increase access to early assessment and diagnosis that will be rigorous and objective. The current study leverages the capabilities of artificial intelligence to develop a reliable and practical model for distinguishing children with ASD from typically-developing peers based on their narrative and vocabulary skills. We applied natural language processing-based extraction techniques to automatically acquire language features (narrative and vocabulary skills) from storytelling in 68 children with ASD and 52 typically-developing children, and then trained machine learning models on the children’s combined narrative and expressive vocabulary data to generate behavioral targets that effectively differentiate ASD from typically-developing children. According to the findings, the model could distinguish ASD from typically-developing children, achieving an accuracy of 96%. Specifically, out of the models used, hist gradient boosting and XGBoost showed slightly superior performance compared to the decision trees and gradient boosting models, particularly regarding accuracy and F1 score. These results bode well for the deployment of machine learning technology for children with ASD, especially those with limited access to early identification services.
